title: Virtual Trade Corridors Could Deepen BRICS Connectivity, Says RITES Chief
excerpt: RITES CMD Rahul Mithal told the BRICS Roundtable that India's MAITRI platform could seed a digital trade network across the bloc — a starting point for the Bharat Trade Net vision.
body:
• RITES chairman and managing director Rahul Mithal told the BRICS Roundtable hosted by the India Today Group that virtual trade corridors — built on shared cargo data — could deepen trade connectivity across BRICS nations even as physical infrastructure takes years to develop.
  • India's MAITRI platform is the template: by sharing cargo information in advance, it lets exporters, importers, ports and customs plan better without replacing existing national systems.
  • Mithal positioned MAITRI as a starting point for the broader Bharat Trade Net vision of a unified digital trade ecosystem.
  • The pitch comes days before the BRICS Summit in New Delhi (September 12–13), with the bloc grappling with conflicts, supply-chain disruptions and tariff tensions.

Can data become the new highway for global trade? At the BRICS Roundtable hosted by the India Today Group, RITES chairman and managing director Rahul Mithal argued that it can — laying out how India's MAITRI platform could underpin faster, more seamless trade corridors across the BRICS bloc.

By sharing cargo information in advance, Mithal explained, the platform helps exporters, importers, ports and customs authorities plan better — without requiring any country to rip out and replace its existing systems. Virtual trade corridors, he said, can bring countries and stakeholders together even as physical infrastructure takes time to develop.

"Can data become the new highway for global trade?"

From MAITRI to Bharat Trade Net

Mithal framed MAITRI — India's maritime and trade information platform — as the starting point for the broader Bharat Trade Net vision: a unified digital ecosystem for trade documentation and logistics. The logic is straightforward. Where new railways, ports and highways take a decade to build, a shared digital layer can start smoothing cargo movement now: fewer paperwork delays, better port scheduling, and customs that sees a shipment coming before it arrives.

With BRICS facing conflicts, supply-chain disruptions and tariff tensions, Mithal's argument is that digital connectivity can still deepen collaboration when the physical and political terrain is difficult. The question posed at the roundtable — can one BRICS network and seamless movement become a reality by 2030? — will be tested against the summit's actual deliverables.

Background: RITES and the corridor business

RITES, the railways consultancy under India's Ministry of Railways, has been expanding its global footprint beyond its traditional African and Southeast Asian markets — winning open-tender orders such as locomotives for Mozambique and coaches for Bangladesh, and conducting feasibility studies on cargo volumes and missing rail links along the proposed India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), the 4,800 km ship-to-rail network announced at the 2023 G20 summit in New Delhi.

Digital trade is now firmly on the BRICS agenda. Reuters reported that India is pushing to link central bank digital currencies across BRICS nations for cross-border payments at this week's summit — a parallel effort to knit the bloc's economies together through shared infrastructure, this time financial rather than logistical.

What's next

India chairs BRICS this year, and the New Delhi summit on September 12–13 will show whether the digital-corridor pitch moves from roundtable advocacy to member-state commitment. For the idea to work, rival systems and wary customs bureaucracies across ten-plus member nations would need to agree on common data standards — the unglamorous plumbing on which seamless trade actually depends.
nri_angle: A domestic trade-infrastructure story; relevant to NRIs in logistics, shipping and trade, and to the diaspora watching India's BRICS chairmanship.
